title: The Brachial Plexus
introduction: The brachial plexus is a somatic peripheral nerve network formed by the ventral rami of spinal nerves C5 to T1 that supplies the muscles and skin of the upper limb[cite: 139, 143, 144]. Organized into roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and 17 branches, it traverses the neck and axilla, making it vulnerable to traction, compression, and birth-related injuries[cite: 145, 148, 151, 152].
learningOutcomes: 2.1 Explain the divisions of the peripheral nervous system and how a typical spinal nerve forms and branches into dorsal and ventral rami[cite: 139, 140, 141, 143].
2.2 Describe the anatomical organization and regional relations of the brachial plexus from roots (C5-T1) to cords and terminal branches[cite: 144, 145, 146].
2.3 Distinguish the muscular compartments supplied by the anterior versus posterior divisions of the brachial plexus[cite: 147].
2.4 List the 17 branches of the brachial plexus according to their origins from roots, trunks, and cords, along with the five main terminal branches[cite: 148, 150].

2.5 Classify brachial plexus injury mechanisms, severity levels (avulsion, rupture, neuroma, neurapraxia), and clinical syndromes including Erb's palsy and Klumpke's palsy[cite: 151, 152, 153, 156, 157].

content.heading: Nervous System Context & Spinal Nerve Formation
content.body: The peripheral nervous system links the central nervous system to the body via the autonomic nervous system (sympathetic and parasympathetic) and the somatic nervous system, which relays sensory input and voluntary motor commands[cite: 139]. Peripheral nerves comprise 12 pairs of cranial nerves from the brain and brainstem and 31 to 33 pairs of segmental spinal nerves (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, and 1 to 3 coccygeal)[cite: 140]. A typical spinal nerve forms by the union of a dorsal root and a ventral root from the spinal cord and emerges through the intervertebral foramen between adjacent vertebrae[cite: 141, 142]. The mixed nerve trunk splits immediately into a dorsal ramus (supplying deeper back muscles and overlying skin) and a ventral ramus (supplying muscles and skin on the lateral and ventral aspects of the body)[cite: 143]. The nerve supply of the limbs is derived entirely from the ventral rami of spinal nerves[cite: 143].

content.heading: Organization & Regional Relations of the Brachial Plexus
content.body: The normal configuration of the brachial plexus is formed by the ventral rami of C5 to T1, which are called the roots of the brachial plexus rather than spinal nerve roots[cite: 144, 145]. These roots emerge from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae immediately posterior to the vertebral artery[cite: 144]. The plexus is organized sequentially into 5 roots (C5-T1), 3 trunks (superior, middle, inferior), 6 divisions (3 anterior and 3 posterior), 3 cords (lateral, posterior, medial), and 5 main terminal branches[cite: 145, 150]. Anatomically, the roots lie between the scalenus anterior and scalenus medius muscles, the trunks lie in the posterior triangle of the neck, the divisions lie behind the clavicle, and the cords and branches are situated in the axilla[cite: 145, 146].

content.heading: Divisions & Functional Distribution
content.body: The three trunks descend laterally above the clavicle and each bifurcates into an anterior division and a posterior division behind the clavicle[cite: 146]. Branches arising from the union of the anterior divisions supply the anterior compartment (flexor) muscles of the upper limb[cite: 147]. Branches arising from the union of the posterior divisions supply the posterior compartment (extensor) muscles of the upper limb[cite: 147].

content.heading: The 17 Branches of the Brachial Plexus
content.body: The brachial plexus gives off a total of 17 branches, plus cervical neck contributions to the scaleni and a branch joining the phrenic nerve to supply the diaphragm[cite: 148]. Root branches (2): long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) and dorsal scapular nerve (C5)[cite: 148]. Trunk branches (2): suprascapular nerve (C5-C6) and nerve to subclavius (C5, C6)[cite: 148]. Lateral cord branches (3): lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6), musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6, C7), and lateral root of the median nerve (C5, C6, C7)[cite: 148]. Medial cord branches (5): medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1), medial cutaneous nerve of the arm (C8, T1), medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm (C8, T1), ulnar nerve (C7, C8, T1), and medial root of the median nerve (C8, T1)[cite: 148]. Posterior cord branches (5): upper subscapular nerve (C5, C6), lower subscapular nerve (C5, C6), axillary nerve (C5, C6), thoracodorsal nerve (C7, C8), and radial nerve (C5, C6, C7, C8, T1)[cite: 148]. The five main terminal branches are the axillary, musculocutaneous, radial, median, and ulnar nerves[cite: 150].

content.heading: Mechanisms & Severity of Nerve Injuries
content.body: Brachial plexus injuries commonly result from contact sports, road traffic or motor vehicle accidents, or birth trauma[cite: 151]. Stretching occurs when the head and neck are forced away from the shoulder (such as a motorcycle fall), producing 'stingers' and 'burners' (pain and burning), and severe traction can avulse nerves from the spinal cord[cite: 152]. Compression can also occur from crushing the plexus between the clavicle and first rib or from local swelling of injured muscles[cite: 152]. Nerve injuries are classified into four levels of severity: avulsion (most severe, where the nerve is torn away from its spinal cord attachment), rupture (the nerve is torn, but not at the spinal cord attachment), neuroma (scar tissue forms around the injured site, compressing the nerve and blocking signal transmission), and neurapraxia (the nerve is stretched or damaged but not torn)[cite: 153].

content.heading: Clinical Conditions Arising from Brachial Plexus Injury
content.body: Erb's palsy (C5-C6 palsy) results from injury to the upper roots during childbirth or trauma, paralyzing the shoulder muscles (deltoid and rotator cuff) and biceps and causing a limp arm with loss of external rotation and flexion[cite: 156]. Klumpke's palsy (C8-T1 palsy) affects the lower roots, usually from trauma, paralyzing the intrinsic hand muscles (thenar eminence and interossei) and forearm flexors, which produces a 'claw hand' deformity with fingers flexed at the knuckles and extended at the interphalangeal joints[cite: 156]. Brachial neuritis presents with sudden, severe shoulder pain followed by progressive arm weakness or paralysis with variable motor and sensory deficits[cite: 156]. Neuroma formation follows rupture or avulsion and causes pain, numbness, or tingling as scar tissue obstructs nerve signals[cite: 157]. Neurapraxia is a mild stretch or compression injury causing transient weakness, numbness, or pain in the shoulder, arm, or hand[cite: 157].

inTextQuestions.question: Which anatomical rami of spinal nerves form the roots of the brachial plexus?
inTextQuestions.answer: The ventral rami of spinal nerves C5 to T1[cite: 144].

inTextQuestions.question: Where are the roots, trunks, divisions, and cords of the brachial plexus anatomically located?
inTextQuestions.answer: The roots lie between the scalene muscles, the trunks lie in the posterior triangle, the divisions lie behind the clavicle, and the cords and branches are situated in the axilla[cite: 145].

inTextQuestions.question: What is the functional difference between branches of the anterior divisions and branches of the posterior divisions?
inTextQuestions.answer: Anterior division branches supply the anterior compartment (flexor) muscles of the upper limb, whereas posterior division branches supply the posterior compartment (extensor) muscles[cite: 147].

inTextQuestions.question: Which type of brachial plexus nerve injury is the most severe?
inTextQuestions.answer: Avulsion, in which the nerve is torn away from its attachment at the spinal cord[cite: 153].

saqs.question: Explain how a typical spinal nerve is formed and distinguish the territories supplied by its dorsal and ventral rami.
saqs.answer: A typical spinal nerve is formed by the union of a dorsal root and a ventral root arising from the spinal cord and exits through the intervertebral foramen[cite: 141, 142]. It immediately divides into a dorsal ramus, which supplies the deeper muscles of the back and their overlying skin, and a ventral ramus, which supplies the muscles and skin on the lateral and ventral aspects of the body—including the entire nerve supply of the limbs[cite: 143].

saqs.question: List the five branches arising from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus along with their root values.
saqs.answer: Upper subscapular nerve (C5, C6), lower subscapular nerve (C5, C6), axillary nerve (C5, C6), thoracodorsal nerve (C7, C8), and radial nerve (C5, C6, C7, C8, T1)[cite: 148].

saqs.question: List the branches arising directly from the roots and trunks of the brachial plexus.
saqs.answer: From the roots: long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) and dorsal scapular nerve (C5)[cite: 148]. From the trunks: suprascapular nerve (C5-C6) and nerve to subclavius (C5, C6)[cite: 148].

saqs.question: Differentiate between avulsion, rupture, neuroma, and neurapraxia in brachial plexus injuries.
saqs.answer: Avulsion is tearing of the nerve away from its spinal cord attachment (most severe)[cite: 153]; rupture is tearing of the nerve away from the spinal cord attachment[cite: 153]; neuroma is scar tissue growth around an injured site that compresses the nerve and blocks signals[cite: 153]; and neurapraxia is stretching or compression without tearing, causing transient dysfunction[cite: 153, 157].

saqs.question: Compare Erb's palsy and Klumpke's palsy in terms of roots affected, muscles paralyzed, and characteristic clinical presentation.
saqs.answer: Erb's palsy involves the upper roots (C5-C6), paralyzes the shoulder muscles (deltoid, rotator cuff) and biceps, and produces a limp arm lacking external rotation and flexion[cite: 156]. Klumpke's palsy involves the lower roots (C8-T1), paralyzes the intrinsic hand muscles (thenar eminence, interossei) and forearm flexors, and produces a 'claw hand' deformity with fingers flexed at the knuckles and extended at the interphalangeal joints[cite: 156].
